caseStudies.title: Removing DTC from a distributed orchestrator
caseStudies.summary: Re-architected a Temporal.io orchestrator to drop its distributed transaction coordinator dependency, unblocking a service estate frozen on legacy .NET runtimes and cutting the upgrade cycle from 5-7 days to 3.
caseStudies.problem: The platform's orchestration layer depended on a distributed transaction coordinator to keep multi-service operations consistent. That dependency pinned services to old runtimes — .NET Core 2.2 and .NET Framework 4.5 — because the coordinator's behaviour could not be carried forward cleanly. Every attempted upgrade risked correctness, so the estate stayed frozen and the cost of change kept rising. Understanding and upgrading a single system cycle took 5 to 7 working days.
caseStudies.approach: I led the re-architecture of the platform's Temporal.io orchestrator so that consistency no longer relied on a distributed transaction coordinator, replacing ambient transactional guarantees with explicit orchestration on its durable-execution model. Rather than treat each service as a one-off, I authored a transformation project template and the rules governing it, so every later module started from a known-good shape instead of a blank page. I then built a set of AI skills and a workflow over them that guided engineers through the transformation — encoding the decisions that were otherwise re-derived by hand on every module. I led the rollout inside my own team and ran sessions with other teams migrating the same way.
outcomes: A single upgrade cycle fell from 5-7 working days to a maximum of 3.
5 modules modernized, with a repeatable template for the rest.
Company award for the resulting time and cost saving.
Other teams adopted the same template and workflow.

caseStudies.title: Making AI usable by engineers and non-engineers alike
caseStudies.shortTitle: Making AI usable across a company
caseStudies.summary: Took AI from ad-hoc use to production: trained non-technical departments (SME recognition), shipped an autonomous Copilot Studio agent, and built the AI-guided workflow that cut upgrade cycles from 5-7 days to 3.
caseStudies.problem: AI tooling was available but unevenly used. Engineers applied it ad hoc with inconsistent results, and non-technical departments such as HR had no route into it at all — the tools assumed a technical vocabulary their work never required.
caseStudies.approach: I treated this as two different problems rather than one. For non-technical staff I designed and delivered a course pitched at their actual workflows instead of at the tooling, which is what earned the subject matter expert recognition. For engineering I went further than training: I built AI skills and an orchestrating workflow that encoded the modernization decisions directly, so the guidance lived in the process rather than in someone's memory. Alongside this I shipped an autonomous agent on Microsoft Copilot Studio, now in production use.
outcomes: Subject matter expert recognition for the AI training course.
Autonomous agent on Microsoft Copilot Studio, in production use.
AI-guided modernization workflow that cut the upgrade cycle from 5-7 days to a maximum of 3.
Development team mentored on applying AI tooling to daily engineering work.

caseStudies.title: Windoor Wizard Builder — a fabrication engine that has to be exactly right
caseStudies.summary: A multi-tenant SaaS for Egyptian UPVC window and door workshops, merging a commercial quoting and production platform with a cutting-optimisation engine verified against a real shop floor.
caseStudies.problem: Egyptian UPVC workshops run on WhatsApp, Excel, and paper. Quotes are priced by hand, cut lists are worked out per job, and the profile offcuts that decide whether a job is profitable are estimated rather than calculated. Generic ERP does not help because it does not model the domain — it has no concept of a frame deduction registry, bar nesting, or the glass area and steel reinforcement that drive real cost. A workshop running generic software still does the hard part on paper.
caseStudies.approach: Three decisions carry this system. First, lengths are stored as exact integer tenths of a millimetre rather than as decimals: the shop cuts half-millimetres — 44 of 195 verified rows — and a rounded cut list produces a window that does not fit. The value type deliberately exposes no decimal factory, so rounding cannot enter the model at all; the wrong thing is unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged. Second, bar nesting is one-dimensional bin packing, so it uses First-Fit-Decreasing, with the three details that separate a real implementation from the textbook one: saw kerf charged per cut, loud failure on a piece longer than a bar rather than a best-effort list that cannot be executed, and a stable sort so two runs over one order produce identical cut lists. Every constant — bar length, end trim, kerf, minimum reusable offcut — is supplied by the caller, so a different workshop is configuration rather than code. Third, the engine became a bounded context inside the SaaS rather than a service beside it, because its calculations always run inside a tenant's quote and share that transaction; a network boundary would have bought overhead and returned nothing. Tenant isolation is enforced by EF Core global query filters, not by a WHERE clause every query is trusted to remember.
outcomes: 491 unit tests passing across domain, application, API, and infrastructure.
Two half-built systems merged into one .NET 10 monorepo: the SaaS had a stubbed pricing engine, the engine had no tenancy or persistence.
Cutting engine oracle-verified against real orders from a working workshop, not against assumptions derived from the same understanding that wrote the code.
72 pre-existing pricing failures kept and documented as the integration specification rather than deleted to make the suite green.
Arabic right-to-left throughout, in the interface and in generated PDFs.

caseStudies.title: One gateway, nine countries
caseStudies.summary: The payment middleware behind Texas Chicken across 9 countries: seven gateways behind a single stateless API — an adapter per gateway, webhooks validated and forwarded, no database. I designed and wrote it; the team lead reviewed and merged.
caseStudies.problem: Payment integration had to work across nine country markets, each with its own providers, rules, and failure modes. Integrating every market directly into the products would have multiplied the same logic seven times over — seven gateway APIs, seven webhook formats, seven credential schemes — and made every provider change a cross-cutting edit.
caseStudies.approach:
I designed the middleware and wrote the code; the team lead reviewed and merged each change. One integration surface speaks to the products; behind it, each gateway lives in its own adapter — Checkout.com, Benefit (Bahrain), Sadad (Qatar), PayMarkClick, MasterCard, and Google Pay and Apple Pay tokenized through MasterCard — resolved by a factory, so adding a gateway means adding an adapter rather than editing shared code. Requests run through MediatR CQRS with validation and logging pipeline behaviors.

The decisive choice was statelessness: no database at all. Client applications keep their own payment state; the middleware generates hosted payment URLs, validates each gateway's webhook signature — SHA-256 and AES for Sadad, SDK-encrypted responses for Benefit, five-layer fraud validation for PayMarkClick — and forwards what is genuine to the client's callback URL. A background worker handles the retries that statelessness still needs. No data stored means nothing to leak, nothing to retain, and horizontal scale by default.
outcomes: 7 payment gateways across 9 countries behind one API.
Designed and shipped in about a month. After I left, I was asked back to add one more gateway for go-live, because I held the full picture.
Stateless by design: zero database, nothing to retain, horizontal scale by default.
Gateway-specific security carried per adapter — encrypted responses, SHA-256 + AES, fraud-validation layers — instead of in shared code.
New gateways onboarded by adding an adapter, without touching shared logic.

caseStudies.title: Rebuilding a legacy MVC application as a .NET Web API
caseStudies.shortTitle: Rebuilding legacy MVC as a Web API
caseStudies.summary: A full rebuild of an ageing MVC application into a modern Web API, including a data access migration from Entity Framework to Dapper and a move onto Azure.
caseStudies.problem: An existing MVC application had accumulated enough structural debt that routine changes were slow and risky. Its data access layer and database schema had grown organically rather than by design, and query performance had become a recurring complaint.
caseStudies.approach: Rather than patch around it, I led a rebuild into a .NET Web API with a redesigned database structure. I replaced Entity Framework with Dapper in the hot paths, trading ORM convenience for explicit control over the SQL where performance mattered. I then supported the migration onto Azure, moving data processing and storage onto managed services.
outcomes: Legacy MVC application replaced by a maintainable Web API.
Query performance improved by moving hot paths from Entity Framework to Dapper.
Database structure redesigned to match how the system is actually used.
Application migrated onto Azure managed services.

caseStudies.title: Four layers between one tenant and the next
caseStudies.summary: A multi-tenant operations platform for real-estate brokerages, which I re-scoped from a single-client build. Tenant isolation is enforced in four independent layers, and every structural decision is written down as an ADR alongside the code.
caseStudies.problem: It began as a build for one brokerage. That client was too small to justify a product on its own, but the problem — leads arriving from Meta, WhatsApp and property portals with no attribution and no follow-up discipline — exists across brokerages in Egypt and the Gulf. Turning it into multi-tenant software put one property above all others: with a single pilot tenant, every isolation mistake stays invisible until the second tenant arrives, and by then the data is already mixed.
caseStudies.approach:
I made tenant isolation an invariant enforced four times over rather than a convention every query has to remember.

The tenant comes only from the authenticated claim, never from a header or a route value. EF Core global query filters are applied by reflection to every tenant-owned entity, so a new table cannot ship without one. PostgreSQL row-level security is forced on every tenant table, driven by a session setting written on each connection open, and the application connects as a role that neither owns the tables nor can bypass the policies; migrations run under a separate owner role. Finally, a SaveChanges interceptor stamps the tenant on every insert and throws on any cross-tenant write.

I rejected query filters alone (one IgnoreQueryFilters call switches them off, and raw SQL never sees them), row-level security alone (a blocked write surfaces as zero rows affected, which reads as success), and a schema per tenant (real migration and connection cost for little gain over row-level security at this stage).

Sign-in, which has to find a user before any tenant is known, goes through one locked-down SECURITY DEFINER lookup instead of an unrestricted connection.
outcomes: 14 architecture decision records written alongside the code, each naming the alternatives it rejected.
Isolation proven by tests, not review: row-level security still blocks access with the EF filters switched off, and the assertions were mutation-tested.
Spreadsheet and CSV imports run in two phases, all or nothing, with caps that refuse zip-bomb workbooks before parsing.
Re-scoped from one client to a product: built once, sold to many brokerages.
Shown here without its name or source code until launch.

caseStudies.title: Setting the architecture of a co-working platform at inception
caseStudies.summary: At the inception of a co-working and entrepreneur-space platform for a Saudi government development bank, across five cities, I wrote and reviewed the SRS, set up the project infrastructure, and drew the architecture a team of five built from.
caseStudies.problem: The platform had to manage rentable offices and co-working spaces across five Saudi cities, with companion apps — 3D mapping of the spaces among them — expected later. The team was small: three backend and two frontend engineers. Before any feature work it needed a specification precise enough to build from, a project structure everyone would share, and an answer to the first structural question: microservices or a modular monolith.
caseStudies.approach:
I wrote and reviewed the Software Requirements Specification and the low-level design, so the business requirements became specifications the team could build from directly. I set up the project infrastructure and drew the architecture and workflow diagrams in draw.io and Mermaid.

On the structural question we chose a modular monolith: a team of five and a modest user base would have paid the operational cost of microservices without collecting the benefit, while clean module boundaries kept the door open for the companion apps to grow out later. In the same period I took over two in-flight projects for maintenance and bug fixing, and studied alongside the work to get ahead of a domain that was new to me.
outcomes: Modular monolith chosen over microservices for a team of 5, with module boundaries that leave room for the companion apps.
An SRS and low-level design the team built from directly.
Project infrastructure and architecture diagrams in place before feature work began.

Led the re-architecture that removed the distributed transaction coordinator (DTC) dependency from a platform's Temporal.io orchestrator, unblocking a service estate frozen on .NET Core 2.2 and .NET Framework 4.5; a single upgrade cycle fell from 5-7 working days to a maximum of 3, recognised with a company award. Authored the transformation template, its governing rules, and an AI-guided workflow that let other teams repeat the migration; 5 platform modules modernized so far. Designs as well as builds: solution architecture documents, SRS and low-level design, Mermaid workflow models, and architecture decision records — including the four-layer tenant isolation of a multi-tenant SaaS now in development. AI that ships: an autonomous Copilot Studio agent in production use, an AI-guided modernization workflow other teams now run, and company-wide AI training (subject-matter-expert recognition).
